code.title: try/except/else/finally order for three cases
code.python:
def demo(kind):
    print("-- case:", kind)
    try:
        print("try: start")
        if kind == "error":
            int("abc")              # raises ValueError
        elif kind == "return":
            return "returned from try"
        print("try: finished")
    except ValueError as e:         # runs only when ValueError was raised
        print("except: caught", e)
    else:                           # runs only when try had no exception
        print("else: no exception")
    finally:                        # always runs, even after return
        print("finally: always runs")
    return "end of function"

for k in ["ok", "error", "return"]:
    print("result:", demo(k))

followUps:
The return in finally wins: it overrides any earlier return and silently swallows any exception that was in flight. Python lets it happen, but it hides real errors, so avoid it (linters flag it).

def f():
    try:
        raise ValueError("lost")
    finally:
        return 42   # f() returns 42, the error vanishes

Python 3.14 even warns about this.

No. os._exit() ends the process immediately, without running finally, cleanup handlers or atexit. A SIGKILL (or power loss) kills the process from outside, so no Python code runs at all.

By contrast sys.exit() only raises SystemExit, so finally does run. Never rely on finally alone for durability; for example write to a temp file and rename it atomically.

A small try block makes it clear which line you expect to fail, so except cannot accidentally catch an error from some other line and hide a bug.

Example: if try: wraps both int(s) and process(n), a ValueError deep inside process is reported as "bad input". Keep only int(s) in the try and put the rest in else.

code.title: Exception vs BaseException and the bare except trap

followUps:
LookupError is the parent of KeyError and IndexError, so except LookupError handles both a missing dict key and a bad list index. OSError (alias IOError, EnvironmentError) is the parent of FileNotFoundError, PermissionError, ConnectionError (and its children such as BrokenPipeError), TimeoutError and IsADirectoryError.

Catch the parent when you treat all children the same, the child when you need a different reaction.

Because cancellation is a signal to stop, not a failure. In 3.8 CancelledError moved from Exception to BaseException so a normal except Exception in your code no longer swallows it and leaves a task that refuses to cancel.

If you must catch it for cleanup, do it in finally or catch it and re-raise. Swallowing it breaks asyncio.timeout(), TaskGroup and shutdown.

code.title: Custom exception hierarchy with pickling and base class

followUps:
Few. Add a class only when a caller would handle that case differently (retry, show a message, abort). If every caller just logs and fails, a single base error with a clear message is enough.

A good test: can you write a distinct except clause for it that does something useful? Carry the variation in attributes (e.code) rather than in dozens of near-identical classes. A handful (3 to 10) per package is typical.

Pickle rebuilds an exception by calling cls(*self.args). If your __init__ takes two parameters but passes one formatted message to super().__init__, then args has 1 item and unpickling raises TypeError (the program above shows it).

This matters in multiprocessing and concurrent.futures, which pickle errors across processes. Fix it by passing the original arguments to super().__init__, or define __reduce__.

Subclass Exception. RuntimeError means "an error that fits no other category", and catching it would also catch unrelated runtime errors such as RecursionError and NotImplementedError, which are its subclasses.

A dedicated base such as class PaymentError(Exception) keeps your hierarchy separate, so except PaymentError catches only your errors. Use RuntimeError as an extra parent only if it truly fits.

code.title: Exception chaining: context, cause, from None

followUps:
Use it when the original error is an implementation detail that would only confuse the caller. The classic case is __getattr__: you look up a key in a dict, get KeyError, and want to raise AttributeError without showing the KeyError.

def __getattr__(self, name):
    try:
        return self._data[name]
    except KeyError:
        raise AttributeError(name) from None

Do not use it when the cause helps debugging.

The original (root) exception is printed first, then the line "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" (or "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred"), then the newer exception last.

So the traceback reads in time order: oldest error at the top, the one that finally escaped at the bottom. When debugging, look at the first block for the real root cause.

code.title: EAFP vs LBYL: isdigit is not int()

followUps:
Classic bug: check then use. The file can be deleted between the check and the open.

if os.path.exists(p):      # check passes
    f = open(p)            # file removed here: FileNotFoundError

Fix: skip the check and try the operation.

try:
    f = open(p)
except FileNotFoundError:
    f = None

The open itself is atomic with respect to the check, so there is no gap another process can use.

hasattr(o, "x") calls the attribute lookup, and in older Python it caught every exception, so a property that raised a real bug (say ZeroDivisionError) made hasattr report False and the bug looked like "missing attribute". Since Python 3 it only swallows AttributeError, but an AttributeError raised inside a property still hides the real fault.

Safer: getattr(o, "x", None) or a try/except AttributeError around the actual use.

No. d[k] += 1 compiles to several steps: read d[k], add 1, store d[k]. A thread switch can happen between read and store, so two threads can both read 5 and both write 6, losing one increment.

Fix it with a threading.Lock around the update, or use per-thread counters and merge, or queue/collections.Counter inside one owner thread. The GIL does not make compound operations atomic.

code.title: Type hints are not enforced at runtime
code.python:
from dataclasses import dataclass, fields

def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

print(add("x", "y"))             # no error: hints are not checked
print(add.__annotations__)       # stored, but only for tools to read

try:
    isinstance([1], list[int])   # runtime cannot check generics
except TypeError as e:
    print("isinstance with list[int]:", type(e).__name__)

@dataclass
class User:                      # dataclass reads the annotations on purpose
    name: str
    age: int = 0

print([f.name + ":" + f.type.__name__ for f in fields(User)])
print(User("Ada", "not a number"))   # still no validation

followUps:
It stops Python from evaluating annotations when the function is defined; they are kept as plain strings instead. That allows forward references (using a class before it is defined) and avoids import-time cost and circular imports.

Type checkers work the same. The catch: tools that need real types at runtime (pydantic, dataclass internals) must resolve the strings with typing.get_type_hints(). In Python 3.14, lazy annotations (PEP 649) make this the default behaviour.

FastAPI reads the annotations of your endpoint function at startup. For def get(item_id: int, q: str | None = None) it sees that item_id is an int and q is optional text, then parses the URL parts, converts "5" to 5, returns a 422 error if conversion fails, and builds the OpenAPI docs.

So the hints do real work at runtime, because the library (via pydantic) chose to read and enforce them.

code.title: Any hides bugs, object forces a check

followUps:
Mostly through code with no annotations (an unannotated parameter or return is implicitly Any), through json.loads() (returns Any), dict.get on an untyped dict, **kwargs without a type, untyped third-party libraries, and from x import * of untyped modules.

Any then flows onward: y = json.loads(s)["a"] is Any, so everything computed from y goes unchecked. Use --strict and warn_return_any to see where it leaks.

Treat the result as untrusted and validate it right away. Light option: annotate as object and narrow with isinstance.

data: object = json.loads(s)
if isinstance(data, dict) and isinstance(data.get("n"), int):
    n = data["n"]

Heavier but safer: a TypedDict or pydantic model that parses the JSON and raises on a wrong shape, giving typed objects for all later code.

code.title: Why list[int] is not list[float]
code.python:
from typing import Sequence

def add_half(xs: list[float]) -> None:
    xs.append(0.5)                 # legal for list[float]

ints: list[int] = [1, 2]
add_half(ints)                     # a type checker rejects this call
print("list of ints is now:", ints)   # a float sneaked in

def total(xs: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return sum(xs)                 # read-only, so int is safe

print(total([1, 2, 3]))            # list[int] accepted as Sequence[float]
print(total((1, 2, 3)))            # tuple[int, ...] accepted too
print(total([1.5, 2]))

followUps:
With covariant=True, or in Python 3.12+ simply by using the new syntax, where the checker infers variance.

T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True)
class Box(Generic[T_co]):
    def get(self) -> T_co: ...

class Box2[T]:   # 3.12: variance inferred
    def get(self) -> T: ...

Covariant is allowed only if T is used in outputs (returns), never as a method parameter.

Keys are used to look values up and must be hashable and comparable. A dict[int, str] can be passed where dict[float, str] is expected only if nothing writes through the reference. A writer could insert key 3.14 into your int-keyed dict.

So the key type is invariant. The value type is invariant too for dict because it is mutable; Mapping[K, V] is covariant in V (read-only) but still invariant in K.

Both are fine; pick one and run it in CI so everyone sees the same results. mypy is the reference checker, with a large plugin ecosystem (Django, pydantic) and incremental caching. pyright is faster on big codebases, has stricter inference, and powers Pylance in VS Code.

They can disagree on edge cases, so do not run both with different configs. Many teams use pyright in the editor and the same tool in CI, or mypy in both.

Options, from cheapest to most work: (1) install a published stub package (types-requests); (2) per-module ignore_missing_imports = true in config, which makes the library Any; (3) write a small .pyi stub file for only the functions you use; (4) wrap the library in one typed adapter module, so the untyped part lives in a single place.

Avoid a global ignore; it silences real typos too.

code.title: unittest: subTest and assertRaisesRegex

followUps:
pytest rewrites the assert statement when it imports your test module, so it keeps the value of each sub-expression and prints them if the assert fails.

assert add(2, 2) == 5
# E assert 4 == 5
# E  + where 4 = add(2, 2)

With plain unittest you would need assertEqual(a, b) to get a similar message. Lists and dicts also get a readable diff of the differing items.

Use pytest.raises with match, which runs a regular-expression search on the message.

with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="must not be negative"):
    parse_age("-1")

To inspect more, use as excinfo and check excinfo.value.args. In unittest the equivalent is assertRaisesRegex, as in the program above. Escape regex characters (re.escape) when the message contains brackets or dots.

code.title: Fixture setup and teardown order (simulated)
code.python:
import contextlib

def db():                               # like a session/module fixture
    print("setup db")
    yield "db-conn"
    print("teardown db")

def txn(conn):                          # like a function-scoped fixture
    print("  setup txn on", conn)
    yield "txn"
    print("  teardown txn")

def use(stack, gen):
    value = next(gen)                   # code before yield = setup
    def teardown():
        for _ in gen:                   # code after yield = teardown
            pass
    stack.callback(teardown)            # ExitStack runs these in reverse
    return value

def run_test(name, test):
    print("test", name)
    try:
        with contextlib.ExitStack() as stack:
            conn = use(stack, db())
            t = use(stack, txn(conn))
            test(t)
    except AssertionError:
        print("  test failed, teardown still ran")

run_test("passes", lambda t: print("  running with", t))
def failing(t):
    assert False
run_test("fails", failing)

followUps:
autouse=True makes a fixture run for every test in its scope without being requested by name. Useful for things every test needs: resetting a global, freezing the clock, blocking network access.

Danger: it is invisible. A reader of the test cannot see it, it adds cost to tests that do not need it, and an autouse fixture in a high-level conftest.py affects hundreds of tests. Use it sparingly and name it clearly.

Pass params to the decorator and read request.param; every test using the fixture then runs once per value.

@pytest.fixture(params=["sqlite", "postgres"])
def backend(request):
    return make_backend(request.param)

With 2 params and 3 tests using it you get 6 test runs. For parametrizing one test only, @pytest.mark.parametrize is simpler.

xdist runs tests in several worker processes. Each worker has its own session, so a "session" fixture runs once per worker, not once per run: a session fixture that creates a database would try to create it N times and clash.

Fix: give each worker its own resource (use the worker_id fixture to name the database, e.g. test_gw0) or guard shared setup with a file lock. Tests must not depend on ordering or shared state.

code.title: Patch the name where it is looked up
code.python:
import sys
import types
from unittest import mock

weather = types.ModuleType("weather")        # the module that defines fetch
weather.fetch = lambda: "real"
sys.modules["weather"] = weather

app = types.ModuleType("app")                # the module under test
exec("""
from weather import fetch    # app gets its own name 'fetch'
import weather
def via_from():  return fetch()
def via_module(): return weather.fetch()
""", app.__dict__)
sys.modules["app"] = app

with mock.patch("weather.fetch", return_value="fake"):
    print("patched weather.fetch ->", app.via_from(), app.via_module())
with mock.patch("app.fetch", return_value="fake"):
    print("patched app.fetch     ->", app.via_from(), app.via_module())

followUps:
Patch the attribute on the class itself, not on an instance. Every instance looks the method up on the class, so all see the mock.

with mock.patch.object(Client, "send", autospec=True) as send:
    Client().send("x")
    send.assert_called_once()

With autospec=True the mock receives self like a real method. To patch one instance only, use mock.patch.object(obj, "send").

Patch the name where the code under test looks it up, i.e. builtins.open, ideally with mock_open.

m = mock.mock_open(read_data="a,b\n")
with mock.patch("builtins.open", m):
    text = read_config("x.cfg")
m.assert_called_once_with("x.cfg")

Better still, use pytest's tmp_path and write a real file; it needs no mock and tests real behaviour.

code.title: Fake vs autospec mock

followUps:
A stub returns canned answers. A fake is a working but simplified implementation (in-memory repository). A spy wraps or records real calls so you can check them afterwards. A mock is pre-programmed with expectations and fails if calls differ.

Example: a stub clock always returns 10:00; a fake repo stores rows in a dict; a spy counts how often send_email was called. In Python unittest.mock.Mock can play any of these roles.

Never call the real API in unit tests: it is slow, costs money and gives different answers each time. Put the call behind a small function or class (llm.complete(prompt)) and in tests replace it with a fake that returns fixed text, including error cases such as timeouts and malformed output.

Then test your parsing, retries and prompt building against those fixed replies. Keep a few clearly marked integration or evaluation tests against the real model, run occasionally rather than on every commit.

code.title: Deterministic retry test: inject sleep, clock and Random

followUps:
Inject the sleep function and replace it with one that records the delays instead of waiting. The test then runs in microseconds and can assert the exact schedule.

slept = []
retry(flaky, attempts=4, sleep=slept.append)
assert slept == [0.1, 0.2, 0.4]

If the code reads the clock, inject that as well, or patch time.sleep and time.monotonic with fakes that advance a counter.

Run the suite in random order (pytest-randomly) and see which order fails. To locate the leaker, bisect: run the failing test with half of the tests that ran before it, then halve again until one remains (pytest-find-dependencies and --lf help).

Typical leaks are module-level globals, caches, environment variables, a changed working directory, and un-restored patches. Fix by using fixtures that undo their changes (monkeypatch, tmp_path).

code.title: ExceptionGroup and except*

followUps:
ExceptionGroup can hold only Exception subclasses. BaseExceptionGroup can also hold BaseException types such as KeyboardInterrupt or CancelledError.

If you create a BaseExceptionGroup whose members are all plain Exceptions, Python automatically gives you an ExceptionGroup. This is why except* Exception works on task failures but must be used carefully with cancellation.

Walk the tree recursively: a group has .exceptions, which may contain more groups.

def log_all(e):
    if isinstance(e, BaseExceptionGroup):
        for sub in e.exceptions:
            log_all(sub)
    else:
        logger.error("failed", exc_info=e)

Alternatively traceback.print_exception(eg) or logger.exception prints the whole nested tree already, with indentation, for a quick answer.
